To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the introduction of a triazole moi-ety into multibranch chromophores substantially modi- fies their optical properties, and (ii) the interplay of don- or/acceptor strength and branching allows for the tuning of the linear and nonlinear optical properties of the chromophores.

the interplay of the donor/acceptor strengths, regioisomerization of the triazole moiety, and branching are demonstrated to be efficient means for precise tuning of one- and/or two-photon absorption in perspective of optical transparency.

The introduction of triazole moieties in multibranched molecules leads to substantial modifications of the electronic delocalization, charge transfer properties between donating end-groups and the branching center, which can be controlled by triazole ring.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new family of triazole based multibranched multipolar chromophoric molecules.
the development of a theoretical framework that will help to understand and predict the structure-property relations of multipolar chromophoric systems.
the design of novel chromophores for nonlinear optics.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, by using the triazole ring as a branching center, it is possible to tune linear and nonlinear optical properties of the chromophores.
triazole-based chromopohores have been designed to be used as nonlinear optical materials for optical limiting.
the triazole moiety is a key component of these chromophores.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the triazole-based multibranched systems are very promising candidates for two photon absorption applications.

the combination of TD-DFT, natural transition orbitals (NTOs), and the Frenkel-exciton model can be used to understand and predict the structure-property relationships of multipolar chromophoric systems.
the triazole ring can be used as a branching center for multibranched molecules and the regioisomer of triazole has a strong influence on the optical properties of these molecules.
The main takeaway from our work is that
isomer position is a critical factor in the design of TPA molecules.
the introduction of triazole units in multibranched systems allows for the control of both linear and two-photon optical responses by tuning their position, regiochemistry, and branching.

, in addition to the well-known branching effect on the optical properties of multibranched molecules, regioisomer positioning of the branching center is another important factor to be considered for optimizing the nonlinear optical responses of these systems.
